newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Battle on WTO farm statement ends in uneasy draw.
newsitem.headline: Battle on WTO farm statement ends in uneasy draw.

text.p: Agricultural powers battled to a standstill over a statement on farm trade at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting before agreeing to a carefully worded compromise, officials said on Friday.
The wrangling over farm trade became a rehearsal for the even tougher bargaining expected when negotiations to further liberalise agricultural trade begin in earnest in 1999.
The row pitted the European Union (EU) against the United States and the Cairns Group of farm exporting countries.

The EU defeated a proposal by Argentina, a member of the Cairns Group, to begin preliminary studies on farm issues in 1997, which the EU saw as a ploy to start early talks over agricultural issues, an Asian diplomat at the talks said.

"We didn't back down to anybody on anything," Canada's Minister for International Trade, Art Eggleton, told Reuters in an interview when asked if the Cairns Group yielded to EU objections over the initial wording of a reference to farming in the WTO declaration.
The Cairns Group links major farming nations including Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Hungary, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Australia, Thailand and Uruguay.
"We agreed to a number of provisions calling for future negotiations on agriculture," said the joint declaration adopted by the WTO's 128 members issued on Friday.
"The Cairns Group is very supportive of paragraph 19 (the agricultural section of the WTO's final declaration). We're quite satisfied," Eggleton said.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer praised the WTO statement, saying it would enable "preparatory work next year for a new round of negotiations on agriculture beginning in 1999".

An Asian diplomat said: "We got a statement on agriculture and the EU managed to remove the Argentinian proposal from the table. But this is just the start of a very painful process over farm issues."

August Schumacher of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Foreign Agriculture Service said: "Some countries, especially the European Union, are concerned that some exporting countries want to move a little faster than they are prepared to move."
He made the comment in Hong Kong on Friday after attending the WTO meeting earlier in the week.
Eggleton said the Cairns Group was planning to issue a separate statement on farm trade to supplement the declaration by the WTO on the issue.

"The gist of that statement is to really deplore the non-compliance of the Uruguay Round agreements on (removing) export subsidies and domestic support," Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista told reporters in a briefing.
"The EU is the biggest violator of agricultural subsidies," he added.
An Asian diplomat said the release of the statement was held up because some countries had yet to sign it.

Liberalising farm trade was one of the most divisive issues in the last round of global trade negotiations, which concluded in 1994. Politically powerful farm groups, especially in France, nearly scuttled the talks then.
